description: I am a CS student working on the space exploration storytelling challenge. My goal is to design an interactive web experience bringing the untold stories of off-world rovers, landers, and probes to life for young space enthusiasts. Looking for creative teammates skilled in UI/UX design, frontend development, or technical storytelling to build a standout portfolio project together!
summary:
Tales of the Red Planet is an interactive, scroll-based children's story that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to NASA's Mars missions that have gone quiet. The story begins when a young girl, Clara, sees a TV news report that the Opportunity rover has gone silent, and she asks why everyone is sad. Opportunity then tells its own story, and Clara reads about Mariner 4, Spirit, Phoenix and InSight: why each was sent, what it did, and where it rests now. She also learns that Perseverance is still working, and that the leopard-spotted rock it found is only a clue to ancient life, not proof. The story ends with Mars inviting the next generation of explorers.

This answers the challenge "Abandoned but not Forgotten" by turning discarded hardware and its science into a short, emotional story with simple facts, illustrated pages and voice narration. It matters because stories help children care about science, and because these machines' discoveries deserve to be remembered.
details:
WHAT IT DOES: Tales of the Red Planet is a scroll-based, illustrated and voiced story for children. It opens with a TV news report that the Opportunity rover has gone silent. A young girl, Clara, asks who Opportunity was, and Opportunity tells its own story in first person: why it was sent, what it found, and how it fell silent in the 2018 dust storm. Clara then reads about Mariner 4, Spirit, Phoenix and InSight (why each was sent, what it did, and where it rests now) and about Perseverance, which is still working. The next day she talks about what she learned with a friend, says she is sad for the quiet robots, and dreams of one day sending a spacecraft to bring Perseverance's rocks home. Mars itself ends the story by inviting the next generation of explorers.

HOW IT WORKS: The story has 16 illustrated pages. Each page shows one picture in a framed scene on a starry background, a short text bubble in the bottom-right corner, and one voice line. Pictures and text fade in and out as the child scrolls (or uses the arrow buttons), and the voice always matches the page on screen. If the child skips ahead or back, the previous voice stops and the new page's voice plays. The text is always visible, so the story also works with sound off.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT: The story introduces real NASA missions and their science (water on Mars, marsquakes, and a "potential biosignature", which is a clue and not proof of life) in simple language. By giving each robot a voice and a feeling, we want children to care about hardware that is usually forgotten once its mission ends, and to feel invited to become the next explorers.

TOOLS AND SOFTWARE: - Website: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no frameworks), hosted on Netlify, code on GitHub.
- Facts and reference photos: NASA mission pages (links listed in the NASA Data section).
- Illustrations: AI-generated with Gemini,ChatGPT, based on real NASA photos. Every AI image carries a visible "AI-generated" label.
- Voices: AI-generated with ElevenLabs.
- Code, story structure and writing help: AI-assisted with Claude (Anthropic).

HOW IT IS CREATIVE: Instead of a list of facts, we told a story with a child's point of view, a news-report opening, robots that speak for themselves, and an ending that passes the question "Was Mars ever alive?" to the reader.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED: - Accuracy: every date and number comes from NASA sources, and we used careful words ("might be a clue, not proof yet") for the life question. - Age-appropriate language: short sentences and gentle words like "went to sleep" or "went quiet". - Honesty: the TV news and the robots' voices are marked as a dramatization, and all AI-generated images, voices and code are labeled. - NASA branding: we did not use any NASA logos or mission patches, and the project is not endorsed by NASA. - Accessibility: text is always on screen, there is a voice on/off button, keyboard navigation, and reduced-motion support.

TEAM AND ROLES:
- Avinash: Contributed to the project concept, code debugging, suggestions, research, and data collection.
- Ayesha: Responsible for voice selection, testing, storyboard development, prompt engineering, and brainstorming.
- Tayyaba: Contributed to the project concept, illustrations, script development, and coding.
All code was written with AI assistance (Claude). Illustrations were created with Gemini and ChatGPT, and voices with ElevenLabs. See the tools list above.
